items.prompt: State what is meant by an equatorial climate.
items.canonical_answer: A hot, wet climate found near the Equator, with temperatures of about 26 to 28 degrees Celsius in every month and heavy rainfall in most months of the year.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - hot and wet all year, near the Equator. "A hot place" alone is not enough without the wetness and the location.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why an equatorial climate has heavy rain most afternoons.
items.canonical_answer: The midday sun is high all year near the Equator, so the ground heats strongly through the morning. The heated air rises, cools and condenses into tall storm clouds, because the air is full of moisture evaporated from the forest and rivers. The clouds then dump their rain in a heavy afternoon downpour, which is why the daily pattern is sunny mornings and stormy afternoons.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: the ground heats because the sun is high; which causes air to rise, cool and condense; so afternoon convectional rainfall results.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table below shows climate data for a weather station in the interior of the Sahara Desert:

| month | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean daily maximum temperature / degrees C | 20 | 23 | 27 | 31 | 35 | 38 | 39 | 38 | 36 | 31 | 25 | 21 |
| rainfall / mm | 5 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 6 |

Describe the climate of this station.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows a hot desert climate. The hottest month is July at 39 degrees Celsius and the coolest is January at 20 degrees Celsius, so the annual temperature range is 39 - 20 = 19 degrees. Rainfall is very low: no month receives more than 6 mm, and from May to August no rain falls at all, with a yearly total of about 24 mm.
marking_guidance: Reading: the overall pattern read from the table - hot, with a large temperature range and very little rain (1 mark).

Figures: the temperature values or the range (39 against 20 degrees) and the rainfall values with their units, so the figures support the words (1 mark), and the six completely dry months identified (1 mark).

items.prompt: In a town deep in the Sahara, the traditional houses have thick mud walls, small windows and flat roofs. Suggest how these three features help people live with the hot desert climate.
items.canonical_answer: The thick mud walls insulate the rooms, so the fierce afternoon heat is kept out and the inside stays cool into the evening. The small windows let in little direct sun and keep out wind-blown sand, which reduces the heat gained during the day. The flat roofs give a place to sleep outdoors on hot nights, when the rooms themselves stay too warm.
marking_guidance: This resource suggests 1 mark per feature explained with its link to the climate, to 3: thick walls insulate, because the desert day is extremely hot; small windows keep out sun and sand; flat roofs provide cooler sleeping at night.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner looking at a climate graph says the rising line across the year must show rainfall, because the wet season is coming. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to mix up the two shapes on the graph: the bars show rainfall in millimetres and the line shows temperature in degrees Celsius, so a rising line means warmer months, not heavier rain. The test before describing any climate graph is to check which axis and which shape carries which variable. Ranges work the same way: the annual temperature range is the warmest month minus the coolest, whereas the daily range is the difference between day and night within one day.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - the line is temperature, not rainfall; the graph reader has read the wrong axis.
1 mark: the correct reading stated instead - bars for rainfall, line for temperature, or the daily range distinguished from the annual range.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes that hot deserts are dry because a cold current of air blows in from the ocean. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is calling the ocean current an air current: the Benguela Current off Namibia is a flow of cold water, not air. It dries the desert because it chills the air above the sea, and cold air holds little moisture, so the onshore winds arrive without rain. The deeper reason deserts are dry is sinking air in high-pressure belts, which keeps clouds from forming; the cold water adds to that, and the test is whether the explanation is about the air, the ocean, or both.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the mistake named - the current is water, not air, so the mechanism was wrongly attributed.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - sinking high-pressure air, plus the cold ocean current cooling the air above it.

items.prompt: A tour company must choose between an equatorial site and a hot desert site for an outdoor football tournament. Suggest which site is the better choice and justify your answer.
items.canonical_answer: The hot desert is the better choice, with the matches played in the cooler months of the year. The judgement rests on rainfall: a desert station receives under 250 mm a year and has months with none at all, so rain is unlikely to stop play, whereas an equatorial station receives over 2000 mm a year and heavy convectional storms most afternoons, which would interrupt the schedule almost daily. The desert's heat is the one drawback, but scheduling early in the day avoids it, while no scheduling avoids the equatorial afternoon storms.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a decision naming the better site.
Reasoning: 1 mark because the choice is argued from rainfall, storms or heat.
Evidence: 1 mark for figures used, such as under 250 mm against over 2000 mm a year, or the afternoon storm pattern.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an ecosystem.
items.canonical_answer: All the plants and animals living in an area, together with the soil, water and climate they depend on.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - living things together with their environment. "Plants and animals" alone is not enough without the environment they interact with.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why the floor of a tropical rainforest is dark and bare.
items.canonical_answer: The tallest trees grow to thirty metres and more, and their crowns meet in a dense canopy. That canopy, with the layers of younger trees beneath it, intercepts most of the sunlight before it reaches the ground, because the leaves are broad and closely packed. In the deep shade on the floor few plants can photosynthesise, so the ground stays bare apart from seedlings waiting for a gap to open when a tree falls.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: the canopy towers above the floor; which blocks most of the light, so less than about 2 per cent of sunshine gets through; and the result is that few plants can grow there.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
Two one-hectare plots were surveyed for a year, one in the Amazon rainforest and one in a hot desert:

| group recorded | rainforest plot | desert plot |
|---|---|---|
| flowering plants | 280 | 9 |
| butterflies | 62 | 5 |
| birds | 92 | 11 |

Describe what the table shows about the two ecosystems.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the rainforest plot holding far more species in every group: 280 flowering plants against 9, 62 butterflies against 5, and 92 birds against 11. The rainforest values are between about eight and thirty times the desert values, which means the rainforest supports a much greater variety of life even over the same area and the same year.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - the rainforest richer in every group (1 mark).
Figures: the values quoted with their groups, so the comparison is backed by figures, and the size of the gap noted (1 mark each for two of these).

items.prompt: A photograph taken in the Namib Desert shows a plant with a fat swollen stem, no visible leaves and a shallow mat of roots just under the surface. Suggest how these features help the plant survive.
items.canonical_answer: The fat stem stores water, which keeps the plant alive through months without rain. With no broad leaves there is little surface for water to evaporate from, so the store is not wasted. The shallow roots spread wide just under the surface, so they can soak up water from a brief shower before it drains away or evaporates, because in a desert the rain seldom soaks in deeply.
marking_guidance: This resource suggests 1 mark per feature linked to survival, to 3: the stem stores water; the absence of leaves cuts water loss; the shallow roots catch brief rain because rain rarely soaks deep.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes that a drip tip on a rainforest leaf helps the leaf hold on to moisture. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is the direction: a drip tip sheds water, it does not keep it. The pointed tip channels heavy rain off the leaf, so the leaf dries quickly instead of collecting water, which would block light and let fungus grow. In a rainforest, water is in oversupply and light is the scarce resource, so the test of any plant adaptation there is whether it removes water or competes for light; buttress roots, which support tall trees in shallow soil, work the same way.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - drip tips shed rain rather than store it.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - heavy rain channelled off, with light or fungus mentioned as the reason.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A conservation charity can put most of its budget into either tropical rainforest protection or hot desert protection. Suggest which ecosystem deserves the larger share, and justify your choice.
items.canonical_answer: The rainforest deserves the larger share. The judgement rests on two pieces of evidence. First, the number of species at risk is far higher: a single hectare of rainforest can hold more than two hundred tree species, against a handful in a desert plot, so the same money protects many more species. Second, clearing rainforest releases stored carbon dioxide, which adds to global warming, so the loss harms the whole planet and not just the forest. Desert ecosystems are fragile too, and recover slowly from damage, but the scale of what is at risk in the rainforest is greater.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for a decision naming the ecosystem that deserves more.
Reasoning: 1 mark because the argument turns on species numbers, carbon, or fragility.
Evidence: 1 mark for figures or examples used, such as two hundred tree species a hectare, or carbon release from clearing.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two benefits that clearing tropical rainforest can bring to a country.
items.canonical_answer: The cleared land becomes farmland for cattle ranching or crops, which creates jobs and export income for the country. Logging the forest first supplies valuable hardwood timber that can be sold abroad, so the clearing pays for itself in the short term.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit taken to its consequence, to 2: farmland, timber, minerals or settlement land, because the benefit earns income or feeds people, which means it counts as a national gain.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two problems that deforestation causes for people living in the cleared area.
items.canonical_answer: The soil loses its fertility: with no tree roots and leaves to protect and feed it, the exposed ground washes away, so crops fail within a few seasons. Flooding also becomes worse, because rain runs off the bare slopes faster and swells the rivers, which threatens villages and fields downstream.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per problem taken to its consequence, to 2: soil erosion, flooding, lost medicines and food plants or lost indigenous land, because each problem harms livelihoods, which means it is felt locally.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how cutting down trees on a rainforest slope can lead to flooding in villages downstream.
items.canonical_answer: The cause is the loss of interception: living trees catch rain on their leaves and take up water through their roots, so when they are removed more rain reaches the ground. Without roots to hold it, the bare soil bakes hard, so the rain runs off the surface instead of soaking in, and the run-off rushes into streams. The effect arrives downstream: streams swell into floods, and villages in the valley are inundated as a consequence of clearing they never saw.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the cause - interception and uptake lost when trees go; 1 mark for the connecting step, so run-off reaches rivers faster; 1 mark for the effect - flooding of villages downstream as the consequence.

items.prompt:
Brazil's space agency estimates the area of Amazon rainforest cleared inside Brazil each year:

| year | area cleared / square km |
|---|---|
| 2004 | about 28 000 |
| 2012 | about 4 600 |
| 2016 | about 8 000 |
| 2021 | about 13 000 |

Describe the trend shown.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows clearing falling steeply between 2004 and 2012, from about 28 000 to about 4 600 square kilometres, a fall of more than 80 per cent. The trend then reverses: the figure rises to about 8 000 square kilometres by 2016 and about 13 000 by 2021, so the overall pattern is a sharp fall followed by a renewed rise, which means the forest came under renewed pressure in the late 2010s.
marking_guidance: Reading: the trend read from the table - a steep fall then a renewed rise (1 mark).
Figures: the values with their years, so both halves of the trend are supported by figures (1 mark for the fall, 1 mark for the rise).

items.prompt: A photograph shows a new road cut through dense tropical rainforest: a wide corridor of felled trees runs to the horizon, trucks are parked along the bare earth, and small cleared plots with new fences spread out from the roadside. Suggest two ways this road could increase deforestation beyond the ground it occupies.
items.canonical_answer: The road gives loggers, cattle trucks and settlers access to forest that was previously too remote to clear profitably, so clearing spreads outward from it. Settlers then clear plots beside the road for farms, because land beside a road can be reached and its produce moved to market, which means the road acts as a spearhead into the forest rather than a single strip of loss.
marking_guidance: This resource suggests 1 mark per way, to 3 marks for a developed pair: access for loggers and ranchers; settlement following the road, because produce can be moved; edges drying out or further tracks branching off.

items.prompt: A question asks for the global effects of tropical deforestation. A learner answers that soil washes away and that rivers flood the villages nearby. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is one of scale: soil erosion and local flooding are local effects, felt in and around the cleared forest, not global ones. The global effects reach the whole planet - burning and rotting cleared vegetation releases carbon dioxide, which adds to global warming, and the species lost with the forest reduce the world's biodiversity. The test is to ask whether each effect stays near the forest or spreads worldwide.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - the effects given are local, not global.
1 mark: the correct global effects instead - carbon dioxide and global warming, or biodiversity loss.

items.prompt: Name the rainforest area you have studied and describe two characteristics that make it distinctive as an equatorial ecosystem.
items.canonical_answer: The Amazon rainforest in South America, the area studied, is the largest area of tropical rainforest on Earth, about 5.5 million square kilometres, of which about 60 per cent lies inside Brazil, and it is distinctive in two ways. Its climate is equatorial, hot in every month and wet in every month, so the forest never faces a dry season. Its structure is layered, a closed canopy with emergent trees above it and shade below, which together with the year-round warmth sustains an enormous number of species, several millions of them, in one ecosystem.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, to 2: the named studied area with its size and location, about 5.5 million square kilometres, about 60 per cent in Brazil; equatorial climate, hot and wet in every month; layered structure or species richness as the characteristics that make it distinctive.

items.prompt: Using a named rainforest area, explain the reasons why its tree cover has been cleared.
items.canonical_answer: In the state of Rondonia in western Brazil, the forest has been cleared because the BR-364 highway, paved in the 1980s, opened the forest to settlement, and access is the first cause: a paved road let migrants and machinery reach land that had been effectively closed. Settlement is the second: migrants arriving along the road cleared plots for small farms, because land along a new highway was cheap and the government's settlement policy encouraged the move. Money from cleared land is the third: logging companies followed to take the hardwood, and cattle ranching spread because pasture could be created cheaply and beef sold at a profit, with soya farms taking over cleared land later. The clearing, in this example, is driven by access, settlement and the profit the cleared ground can be made to pay.
marking_guidance: This example earns 1 mark per developed cause, to 4: the BR-364 highway opened the forest, so access came first; settlers cleared plots, because the settlement policy and cheap roadside land drew them; logging and ranching paid, because beef and timber sell; soya on the cleared land, or the policy behind it, developed as the extra point.

items.prompt: For an area of hot desert you have studied, describe two of its main features.
items.canonical_answer: The Namib runs along the Atlantic coast of southern Angola, Namibia and the Northern Cape for about 2000 kilometres, and is counted among the oldest deserts on Earth. Rainfall near the coast is usually under 20 mm a year, but fog drifting inland over the cold Benguela Current dampens the coast on up to 180 days a year.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, to 2: the long narrow coastal location (about 2000 km); rainfall usually under 20 mm a year; fog on up to 180 days a year; the cold Benguela Current; any valid characteristic of the studied desert.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For an area of hot desert you have studied, explain why people live and work where they do in it.
items.canonical_answer: In the Namib, water decides where people can live. Topnaar communities herd goats along the dry Kuiseb valley, because floodwater lingering under the sand supports the grasses their animals need, and boreholes supply homesteads far from any river. The uranium mine at Rossing near Arandis, running since 1976, draws workers and its town to a spot chosen for the ore, with water bored from underground. Tourism gathers at Sossusvlei, where the dunes above 300 metres draw visitors to the Namib-Naukluft area, so this example shows settlement clinging to water, ore and views.
marking_guidance: This example earns 1 mark per developed point, to 4: herding along the Kuiseb because water lingers there; boreholes supplying scattered homesteads; the Rossing mine (since 1976) drawing workers to Arandis; tourism at the Sossusvlei dunes.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.5 claim ledger.

items.prompt: For a named area of hot desert you have studied, explain how people use the desert and assess how successfully they have overcome its challenges. [7]
items.canonical_answer: The Namib runs along Namibia's Atlantic coast, a desert where rainfall near the coast is usually under 20 mm a year and the only regular moisture is fog on up to 180 days a year. People use it in three main ways. The uranium mine at Rossing, near Arandis, has operated since 1976 and supports a purpose-built town; mining has overcome the desert because ore and water can be found underground and piped to the site. Tourism gathers at Sossusvlei, where dunes above 300 metres draw visitors to the Namib-Naukluft area, and the tour roads and lodges bring income to a place with no farmland. Herding is harder: Topnaar families graze goats along the Kuiseb valley, where floodwater under the sand grows grass and the nara melon, but the herds stay small and the life marginal. The judgement is that the desert is used successfully where water can be engineered - boreholes, pipes and fog - while uses that depend on rainfall alone stay limited, so success has been partial.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about desert life, with no named example or only general points about heat and dryness.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named desert; capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - the Namib, Rossing since 1976, the Kuiseb, the 300 m dunes at Sossusvlei, the fog figures - covering uses and an assessment of the challenges, developed towards a judgement.

items.prompt:
The table below gives climate data for two weather stations. Station A lies near the Equator in the Amazon basin; station B lies in the interior of the Sahara.

| month | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean temperature / degrees C | 26 | 26 | 27 | 27 | 27 | 27 | 27 | 28 | 28 | 27 | 27 | 26 |
| rainfall / mm | 260 | 280 | 300 | 290 | 250 | 170 | 130 | 110 | 120 | 140 | 160 | 210 |

| month | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean daily maximum temperature / degrees C | 20 | 23 | 27 | 31 | 35 | 38 | 39 | 38 | 36 | 31 | 25 | 21 |
| rainfall / mm | 5 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 6 |

(a) Identify the wettest month at station A. [1]
(b) Describe the temperature pattern shown for station A. [2]
(c) Suggest why station A receives heavy rainfall in most months. [3]
(d) Suggest why the rainfall at station B is so low. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) March, with 300 mm.
(b) The table shows station A staying between 26 and 28 degrees Celsius in every month of the year, so its annual temperature range is 28 - 26 = 2 degrees, which is far smaller than the range at station B.
(c) Station A lies near the Equator, where the midday sun is high in every month, so the ground is heated strongly all year. Air heated at the surface rises, cools and condenses, because the air is moist from the forest and the rivers, and the storm clouds give heavy convectional rainfall. In the wettest months, such as March with 300 mm, this process works at full strength.
(d) Station B lies deep inside a continent, far from the sea, so moist winds lose their water long before reaching it. The air over it is also sinking in a high-pressure belt, which keeps clouds from forming, so there is little rain to fall.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) 1 mark for the correct month read from the table, with the 300 mm value.
Figures: (b) 2 marks - the steady pattern described with values (26 to 28 degrees Celsius) and so the small range stated.
Marks: (c) 3 marks - the high midday sun, rising air with cooling and condensation, and the moisture source, developed with evidence such as the March figure.
(d) 2 marks - distance from the sea and sinking high-pressure air, each linked to the lack of clouds; figures such as the six dry months strengthen the evidence.
